records.name: Iowa
records.summary:
Iowa enacted a public-facility-use law in 2023 and bans state-funded gender-affirming care for minors; a September 2026 status check confirmed both remain in force, while the Iowa Supreme Court struck down the parallel ban on surgery coverage for adults — a partial carve-back.

An independent July 2026 legal-risk assessment lists Iowa among its 'worst states' group for transgender adults.

Independent analysts of the same period caution that legal-risk grades predict how the state behaves toward trans people, not how residents do, and that recorded violence counts are undercount floors.

freshness.fact: 2023 bathroom bill + minor care ban remain in force; nuance: Iowa Supreme Court struck down the ban on surgery coverage for adults.

records.name: South Carolina
records.summary: 2024 facility ban expanded in 2026 to colleges and universities, raising its tier to “Worst Laws Passed” in the July 2026 assessment; part of the 18-state birth-sex-definition group. Below the national score 0.36.

records.name: Florida
records.summary:
Florida's 2023 law (Fla. Stat. 553.865) makes it a second-degree criminal trespass — up to 60 days — to remain in a public bathroom or changing facility that does not match sex assigned at birth after a government employee orders departure; the ACLU of Florida calls it 'complex, confusing, and vague' and of limited actual coverage, and among at least 14 states with facility restrictions only Florida and Utah criminalise the act itself.

In March 2025 a 20-year-old trans student was arrested using a women's restroom in the State Capitol — believed the first arrest anywhere under a state bathroom ban. A Leon County judge dismissed the charge in June 2025 on speedy-trial grounds after the state missed a 90-day filing deadline; because the arrest was booked as trespass, the ban's constitutionality was never reached. Equality Florida and the Human Rights Campaign have issued named travel advisories warning of risks to trans travellers and movers.

Physical safety is comparatively better than the law suggests: a July 2026 analysis puts Florida's recorded killing rate for trans women at 3.7 per 100k per year, below the average of the worst-law states — itself an undercount floor.

records.name: Nebraska
records.summary: Gubernatorial executive order narrowing “male”/“female” and ending state recognition of trans people — mostly resident-facing, but it signals an administration willing to use state machinery against gender identity. Below the national score 0.36.

records.name: Kentucky
records.summary:
Kentucky enacted a school-focused facility restriction in 2023 (K-12), recorded in two national trackers of transgender facility-access laws. Both tracker pages have since become unreachable at their cited URLs, so the entry rests on the research dossier's verbatim extract — the weakest evidentiary basis on this map.

For a visitor, direct exposure is limited by the law's school setting, but the statute places Kentucky in the group of states that have legislated against transgender facility use.

records.name: North Carolina
records.summary: The archetype of legislative instability: HB 2 (2016) restricted bathrooms to birth-certificate sex and was repealed in 2017 after mass backlash, but a binary-“sex” statute remains. Trans-murder monitoring data places North Carolina at about 3.0 killings per 100k trans women — a recorded floor, mid-pack among states with documented killings — and the July 2026 legal-risk map classifies it moderate-risk (alongside Alaska and Kentucky). Below the national score 0.36.

records.name: Montana
records.summary:
Montana has passed laws that would grade among the country's worst — including a facility-use ban and a public-buildings bathroom ban — but state courts have repeatedly blocked or enjoined them under the state constitution, leaving little of the anti-trans statutory book in force.

That makes Montana the anomaly of the 2026 legal-risk assessments: the only state whose risk grade was lowered — from 'worst laws' to 'high risk' — by cumulative court rulings and injunctions, in the February 2026 cycle. Statutory risk is high; enforcement risk is genuinely mixed.

records.name: Missouri
records.summary: Bans gender-affirming medical care for minors (the SAFE Act, in force since 28 August 2023 after a judge declined to block it) and restricts access to such treatment for people in prisons, jails and correctional centres, with providers facing licence revocation; no adult facility ban recorded. Slightly below the national score 0.36.
